\section[fiel]{fiel — faithful, loyal}

\label{lesson:ES-C725-fiel}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for sincere, then the Spanish for honesty.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fiel}
\textbf{fiel} — \textquotedblleft{}faithful, loyal\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi perro es muy fiel.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My dog is very faithful.}
\end{quote}

Plural \emph{fieles}; \emph{los fieles} are the faithful in a church.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{fiel} is inherited from Latin \emph{fidēlis} \textquotedblleft{}faithful\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{fidēs} \textquotedblleft{}faith, trust\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{fiel}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{fiel}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{fiel}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for sincere, then the Spanish for honesty, then say \emph{fiel} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does fiel mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Faithful, loyal\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[leal]{leal — loyal}

\label{lesson:ES-C725-leal}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for honesty, then the Spanish for faithful.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: leal}
\textbf{leal} — \textquotedblleft{}loyal\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Siempre ha sido leal a sus amigos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He has always been loyal to his friends.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Leal a} — loyal to.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{leal} is usually traced to Latin \emph{lēgālis} \textquotedblleft{}of the law\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{lēx} \textquotedblleft{}law\textquotedblright{}; English \emph{loyal} and \emph{legal} are the same Latin word by two roads.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la lealtad]{la lealtad — loyalty}

\label{lesson:ES-C725-lealtad}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for faithful, then the Spanish for loyal.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la lealtad}
\textbf{la lealtad} — \textquotedblleft{}loyalty\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Valoro la lealtad por encima de todo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I value loyalty above everything.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{lealtad} is built on \emph{leal} \textquotedblleft{}loyal\textquotedblright{} with the ending \emph{-tad}; EtymDB traces its Portuguese twin \emph{lealdade} to Medieval Latin \emph{lēgālitās}, from \emph{lēgālis} \textquotedblleft{}of the law\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[reconciliarse]{reconciliarse — to make up, to be reconciled}

\label{lesson:ES-C725-reconciliarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for loyal, then the Spanish for loyalty.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: reconciliarse}
\textbf{reconciliarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to make up, to be reconciled\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Después de la pelea, nos reconciliamos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{After the fight, we made up.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Reconciliarse con alguien}. Colloquially \emph{hacer las paces}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{reconciliarse} is usually described as a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{reconciliāre} \textquotedblleft{}to bring together again\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{conciliāre} \textquotedblleft{}to unite\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[fingir]{fingir — to pretend, to fake}

\label{lesson:ES-C725-fingir}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for loyalty, then the Spanish for to make up.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fingir}
\textbf{fingir} — \textquotedblleft{}to pretend, to fake\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Fingió que no me veía.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He pretended not to see me.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Fingir que} + indicative. Spelling: \emph{finjo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{fingir} comes from Latin \emph{fingere} \textquotedblleft{}to shape, to invent, to feign\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB); English \emph{fiction} and \emph{feign} share it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
